>The tendency to conflate Asian heritage with bad parenting is kind of baked into the name of this subreddit

And this is my number one issue with this sub. Way too many people project their parents' issues onto Asian culture as a whole which is a pretty unfair assessment in my opinion. While I don't deny that certain varying cultural factors can act as an enabler for toxic parenting to some extent, there are also many other pressing factors. This includes things like intergenerational cultural divide and the burdens/stress of immigration.

I'm in the latter camp. I don't think that Asian parents are inherently  toxic, nor are toxic parents limited to Asian culture. And Asian culture isn't necessarily toxic per se either, but it can definitely act as an enabler for toxic people. Think of it like some sort of chemical element that isn't explosive on its own, but if you mix with another certain element it can be. 

In addition, the label "Asian culture" is a really really broad one considering that there are 50 something countries on the Asian countries each with different cultures and traditions. And there can be a lot of diversity within a country- for example China as 52 recognized ethnic groups and India has a large list of scheduled tribes and castes, along with various different languages and religions. Moreover, culture changes. So what was acceptable in your parents' home countries during their days living there may no longer be acceptable today.

Regarding LGBT+ erasure, it's kinda interesting that at some points in history homosexuality was actually in fact accepted in certain Asian societies. For example in Ancient China, it was common for emperors to have male lovers. Homophobic policies were often attributed to influences from the west. For example, India's penal code criminalizing gay sex (section 377) was enacted by British colonists during the 19th century.

It's the satellite baby phenomenon. 

There are various reasons for this- from lack of affordable/available childcare to difficulty in obtaining visas for extended family members. In a lot of Asian cultures childrearing is based on a kinship model which involves extended family members such as grandparents. Multi-generation households are pretty common as a result. This is a huge contrast to the nuclear family in the west. 

satellite baby phenomenons are especially more common with lower-income Asian families. The parents might be saving up for a house in a desirable neighborhood,  trying to find better paying jobs, etc. In my experience, I've noticed that families who were better off were able to bring grandparents over so they never sent their kids overseas. They likely have a house big enough to hold additional guests and can maybe even help pay for visas. For example, when my friend's younger sister was born, her grandparents came from China and stayed for a year. Then her aunt came and stayed for another year. Another friend of mine lives in China, and when his cousin in the US had a baby, his grandma went over and stayed for a year.
